definition: A category of AI systems that create new content — text, images, code, audio, or video — rather than simply analyzing or classifying existing data.
analogy: Like the difference between an art critic and an artist. Traditional AI is the critic (it analyzes and classifies); generative AI is the artist (it creates something new).
use_in_a_sentence: Our marketing team uses generative AI to draft initial versions of ad copy, which a human editor then refines and approves.
business_context: Generative AI is the fastest-adopted technology in business history. It is transforming content creation, software development, customer service, and research workflows.

definition: A very large AI model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many different tasks — like GPT, Claude, or Gemini. It serves as the 'foundation' that specialized applications are built on top of.
analogy: Like a liberal arts education. A broad foundation of knowledge that can be applied to many careers. You do not retrain from scratch for each job — you specialize based on the foundation.
use_in_a_sentence: Rather than building our own model, we chose a foundation model from a major vendor and customized it for our industry through fine-tuning and RAG.
business_context: Foundation models are the building blocks of modern AI strategy. The key decision is build vs buy — most companies build on top of existing foundation models rather than creating their own.

definition: A type of generative AI that creates images (or other media) by starting with random noise and gradually refining it into a coherent output, guided by a text description or other input.
analogy: Like a sculptor starting with a rough block of marble and gradually chipping away to reveal a detailed statue. The model starts with noise and progressively shapes it into a clear image.
use_in_a_sentence: The design team uses a diffusion model to generate concept art from text descriptions, producing dozens of options in minutes instead of days.
business_context: Diffusion models power tools like DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion. They are transforming graphic design, advertising, and product visualization.

definition: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — a training technique where human raters judge the quality of a model's outputs, and those judgments are used to make the model's responses more helpful, harmless, and honest.
analogy: Like a new employee learning from performance reviews. Managers (human raters) evaluate the employee's work, and the employee adjusts their approach based on what gets praised versus what gets corrected.
use_in_a_sentence: The vendor explained that their model went through RLHF to reduce harmful outputs, which is why it refuses certain types of requests.
business_context: RLHF is a key reason modern AI assistants feel more helpful and safe than earlier models. It is expensive (requires human raters) but critical for commercial AI products.

definition: An AI model that can understand and generate multiple types of content — such as text, images, audio, and video — within a single system, rather than being limited to just one type.
analogy: Like a multilingual person who can read, write, and speak in several languages. A multimodal model is 'fluent' in text, images, and sometimes audio or video simultaneously.
use_in_a_sentence: We chose a multimodal model so our customer support bot can understand both text messages and uploaded photos of damaged products in the same conversation.
business_context: Multimodal capabilities are becoming standard in leading AI models. They open up use cases like visual question answering, document understanding, and video analysis.

definition: An AI system that can independently plan and execute multi-step tasks by using tools, making decisions, and taking actions — going beyond just answering questions to actually doing work.
analogy: Like the difference between asking someone for directions versus hiring a driver. A chatbot gives you directions; an AI agent drives you there, handling navigation, traffic, and detours on its own.
use_in_a_sentence: We deployed an AI agent that handles the entire refund process — it looks up the order, checks the policy, processes the return, and emails the customer, all without human intervention.
business_context: AI agents represent the next wave of automation beyond chatbots. They can handle complex workflows but require careful guardrails to prevent costly mistakes.

definition: Artificially generated data that mimics the statistical properties of real data. Used when real data is scarce, expensive to collect, or contains privacy-sensitive information.
analogy: Like flight simulator hours for pilots. The scenarios are not real flights, but they are realistic enough to build genuine skills. Synthetic data trains models without exposing real information.
use_in_a_sentence: Because healthcare regulations limited our access to real patient data, we used synthetic data to train and validate the model before testing on actual records.
business_context: Synthetic data solves two major problems: data scarcity and data privacy. It is increasingly used in healthcare, finance, and any domain with strict data regulations.

definition: Rules, filters, and safety mechanisms built around an AI system to prevent it from producing harmful, inappropriate, or off-topic outputs. They define what the AI should and should not do.
analogy: Like the bumper rails in a bowling alley lane for kids. The ball (AI output) can still roll freely, but the rails prevent it from going into the gutter (producing harmful or irrelevant content).
use_in_a_sentence: We implemented guardrails that prevent our customer-facing chatbot from discussing competitors, making promises about pricing, or sharing internal company information.
business_context: Guardrails are essential for any customer-facing AI deployment. Without them, models can generate responses that create legal liability, brand damage, or customer harm.
